title: Make housing a basic right in the Constitution
detail: Change the Constitution so housing becomes a fundamental right (*derecho fundamental*). Citizens could then take the authorities to court to claim it. The programme does not explain the voting process.
c: Today the right to housing is one of the guiding principles (art. 47). Moving it to the fundamental rights needs the art. 168 process: two-thirds of both chambers, a new election, a new vote and a referendum. This is not possible without PP, which is against it.

s.t: Spanish Constitution, art. 47 (BOE)
Spanish Constitution, art. 168 (BOE)

title: CASA 47: 100,000 public homes
detail: The state housing company CASA 47 (created at the end of 2025) would build and buy 100,000 homes. It would sell them or rent them long-term at affordable prices, in addition to regional and town-hall housing. Its income goes back into housing, and public land goes into a land bank for social housing groups and housing co-ops.
c: The company exists, but 100,000 homes in four years is optimistic. That is about all the homes Spain finishes in one year (100,980 in 2024). Existing public land and SAREB homes would come first, and new building takes years.
pos: A permanent group of affordable rental homes, like in Vienna and the Basque Country, keeps prices lower in the long term and never goes back to the open market.
neg: 100,000 homes is about 0.5% of main homes (about 19.7 million households, INE), so the effect on prices is small and slow. Buying finished homes means competing with other buyers, which can push prices up.

s.t: Housing Ministry: Observatorio de Vivienda y Suelo, annual bulletin 2024 (La Moncloa)
INE: population and households at 1 Jan 2026 (ECP)

title: Stop rents from rising above the official price index
detail: For a time, stop rents in stressed markets from going above the official price index (*índice de referencia*). The programme gives no limit or formula. The Housing Ministry would publish its own map of stressed areas (*zonas tensionadas*). Under the 2023 Housing Law the regions should make this map, but many do not.
c: The Housing Law already allows rent limits, but only where a region has named a stressed area, and regions run by PP do not. No formula is given. Studies in Catalonia find rents 4 to 6% lower, but they disagree on whether fewer homes were offered for rent.
pos: It protects tenants from big rises in the cities with the highest demand.
neg: Rent limits do hold prices down: studies in Catalonia find rents 4 to 6% lower. But one study sees more expensive homes leave the rental market, and after the 2024 limits the number of rental ads fell by about 20% (Fedea estimate). In Berlin, rents just outside the city went up sharply.

s.t: Ley 12/2023 on the right to housing (BOE)

title: Tax on "vulture funds" and large landlords
detail: A tax that rises with the number of homes, for large landlords (*grandes tenedores*) and investment funds (*fondos buitre*, "vulture funds"), unless they rent the homes long-term at affordable prices. It would apply to homes used as tourist flats, homes left empty and homes rented at "excessive" prices. The programme gives no limits or rates.
c: The tax needs an ordinary law, but also a majority, and Junts is against it. Regions run by PP can cancel similar taxes in their area. Courts could also see it as charging the same tax twice.
pos: It gives owners a reason to rent out or sell empty homes, and it brings money for housing policy.
neg: Funds own only a few per cent of all homes. Landlords will pass part of the tax on to tenants, and investors may stop building homes for rent.

title: TU CASA: interest-free loans of up to €50,000 for a first home
detail: A €10 billion fund for loans of up to €50,000 with no interest to buy a first home (*primera vivienda*). It is for people with a stable income but no savings. If the money runs out, the fund would get more. The programme gives no income limits.
c: A €10 billion fund through the state bank ICO is realistic. But a 0% loan for the deposit means more buyers while there are too few homes, and that will raise prices.
pos: The loan takes the place of savings people do not have, so it is easier for young people to buy a first home.
neg: More buyers without more homes means higher prices. The state takes the risk if people do not pay back.

title: Raise tax on large investment income to 35%
detail: Income from savings and investments (*rentas del ahorro*) keeps its first two bands: 19% up to €6,000 and 21% up to €50,000. Above that, the rates go up step by step to 35% on investment income over €300,000 (today the rate at that level is 30%).
c: It is a technically simple change to income tax. But it needs a majority in Congress, and PSOE often did not have one in the last four years. Money moves easily, so some of this income will move into structures with lower tax.
pos: It is fairer: rich people's investment income would pay almost the same tax as wages.
neg: Money moves easily. Some of it will go abroad or into holding companies, so the state may get less than it expects.

title: Child tax credit paid even to families who owe no tax
detail: Change the tax-free amount for children (*mínimo por descendiente*) into a tax credit that the state pays out even when a family owes no tax. Then about 2 million families on low and middle incomes, who do not file a tax return or owe no tax, could use it.
c: It is technically simple, and the system already exists for mothers of children under 3. The cost is moderate: in our estimate, from a few hundred million to €1 billion.
pos: Money for low-income families who cannot use the tax-free amount today. It works well against child poverty.
neg: It costs up to about €1 billion a year. If it is paid in advance each month, some families may get too much and have to pay it back later.

s.t: Ley 35/2006 on income tax, maternity deduction (BOE)

title: Put pensions that rise with prices into the Constitution
detail: Write into the Constitution that the public pension system is protected and that pensions rise with consumer prices (*IPC*). Today an ordinary law guarantees the price link.
c: A change to the Constitution under art. 167 needs three-fifths of both chambers (210 deputies), which is not possible without PP. PP supports linking pensions to prices, so the parties could agree on the idea, but politically it is unlikely.

s.t: Spanish Constitution, art. 167 (BOE)

title: A law to keep the minimum wage at 60% of the average wage or more
detail: Write in law that the minimum wage (*SMI*) cannot be lower than 60% of the average wage. It would be updated for prices, wages and productivity. Employers could not cancel out a rise by cutting other pay extras (*absorción de complementos*). The SMI is €1,221 today.
c: The SMI is already close to the 60% goal (€1,221 × 14 payments in 2026). Writing it into law is realistic. Critics say that in poorer regions this level is harder to pay.
pos: Low earners keep up with prices, and fewer working people live in poverty.
neg: In poorer regions and small businesses, 60% of the national average wage is a lot. Some jobs could be lost or move to work without contracts.

s.t: Real Decreto 126/2026: 2026 minimum wage of €1,221 a month (BOE)

title: A 37.5-hour working week with the same pay
detail: Finish cutting the working week to 37.5 hours, and encourage collective agreements to reach 35 hours, with no loss of pay. Unions, employers and the government would agree a timetable, with extra time for small businesses (*pymes*). No date is given.
c: On 10 September 2025 Congress sent the 37.5-hour bill back to the government (changes proposed by PP, Vox and Junts). It could pass only with a different balance of seats. The employers' organisation CEOE is against it.

s.t: Congress, BOCG 15-A-58-3: 37.5-hour bill returned to the government (10 Sep 2025)

title: *Autónomos*: social security fees based on real income
detail: Update the law for self-employed workers (*Estatuto del Trabajo Autónomo*). Continue the move to fees based on real income (*cotización por ingresos reales*), and make it easier for self-employed people to get unemployment benefit (*cese de actividad*). The programme gives no amounts.
c: Fees based on real income are already coming in step by step from 2023 to 2032. Continuing is realistic.
pos: Fairer fees: people who earn little pay less, and people who earn a lot pay more.
neg: *Autónomos* who earn more will pay more. It is harder for people whose income changes a lot from month to month.

s.t: Real Decreto-ley 13/2022: self-employed contributions and flat rate (BOE)

title: End waiting lists: about 7% of GDP for public health
detail: Keep public health spending at about 7% of GDP, make the public National Health System (*SNS*) stronger, and slowly raise spending on prevention to the European average. No timetable or amount in euros is given.
c: Public health spending is already about 6.5 to 7% of GDP, so the target is almost reached. Waiting lists depend on the regions and the lack of doctors, not on a share of GDP.
pos: Stable money for health care and shorter waits.
neg: The regions run the system and may just use state money instead of their own. The programme names no source of money.

s.t: Eurostat, gov_10a_exp: Spain's public health spending, % of GDP (2022–2024)

title: The state takes over €83 billion of regional debt
detail: The state takes over part (*asunción parcial*) of the regions' debt (*deuda autonómica*), €83 billion, to help regional finances. The programme does not say how much each region gets or on what conditions.
c: In December 2025 the government sent parliament a bill to cancel €83 billion of debt. It is an organic law (176 votes). Junts has doubts, and regions run by PP say no, because they see it as a gift to ERC. State debt grows by the same amount.
pos: Regions with a lot of debt (Catalonia, Valencia, Andalusia) get more money to spend on services.
neg: Regions that borrowed more get more, which rewards borrowing. The debt does not disappear: it moves to the state.

s.t: Finance Ministry, 9 Dec 2025: bill to write off €83,252 million of regional debt sent to parliament
Spanish Constitution, art. 81 (BOE)

title: Keep the plan to close nuclear plants by 2035
detail: Keep the current timetable to close the nuclear plants (*calendario de cierre nuclear*) by 2035, and pay for "just transition" projects in the areas affected. No new plants.
c: The timetable can stay, but Almaraz can already run until 2030 because its owners asked. In our estimate, closing 7 GW without other stable power would raise prices and make Spain use more gas.
pos: No new nuclear waste, and more space on the grid for renewable energy.
neg: About a fifth of Spain's electricity (19% in 2025, REE), stable and free of emissions, disappears. Prices and emissions could rise if the replacement (storage, grids, gas) is not ready.

s.t: Orden TED/864/2026: Almaraz extended to 8 June 2030 (BOE)
